raw_response:
# Authentik federation versus separate passwords and 2FA

Moving login to Authentik does not inherently give every application the same reusable credential. OpenID Connect distinguishes the identity provider, each relying application, and the ID token issued for that application; OAuth access tokens have a separate resource-access purpose. A token should only be accepted by its intended recipient. This makes the phrase “one stolen token” too broad to determine the impact. The relevant token might be an application session cookie, an application-specific ID/access token, a refresh token, or Authentik's own browser session. [OpenID Connect Core](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0-errata1.html) and [Authentik's provider documentation](https://docs.goauthentik.io/add-secure-apps/providers/oauth2/) establish those protocol roles.

The central risk is a shared authentication authority. My inference is that an attacker holding a usable Authentik session may obtain access to additional applications wherever their policies accept that session without fresh verification. Compromise of the identity provider's administrative or signing authority is a broader failure again. By comparison, genuinely independent service passwords and second factors can contain a single service-account compromise, assuming the other credentials and recovery paths remain independent. Neither architecture supplies a universal security ranking without knowing the applications, their session handling, and the attack being considered.

## Ranked reusable designs and mechanisms

### 1. OpenID Connect Core 1.0: application-specific identity tokens and reauthentication

URL: https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0-errata1.html

Use this standard to check whether each application has its own client registration, validates the intended audience, and requests fresh authentication for sensitive access. The ID token's audience includes the relying party's client ID, while max_age and auth_time support an explicit freshness requirement. This directly addresses whether a token stolen from service A should work at service B.

Caveat: an ID token is not an access token or a universal session cookie; merely using a JWT does not establish correct recipient validation. Freshness also depends on what authentication the provider actually requires.

Date evidence: the opened errata-1 specification is dated 8 November 2014, before the 28 March 2025 cutoff.

### 2. Authentik Authenticator Validation stage: retain mandatory MFA centrally

URL: https://docs.goauthentik.io/add-secure-apps/flows-stages/stages/authenticator_validate

This component helps preserve the existing second-factor requirement when moving authentication into Authentik. Its configurable device classes, enrollment behavior, and last-validation threshold let the authentication flow require an accepted factor and control when a recent verification may be reused. For accounts with no eligible authenticator, configure enrollment or denial instead of allowing the flow to skip MFA.

Caveat: placing MFA in a login flow does not prove that every application access reruns it. Verify the relevant provider flow and session behavior; an already-authorized application session can have its own lifetime. Authentik's [hardening guidance](https://docs.goauthentik.io/security/security-hardening) also calls out recovery flows as part of the account's security boundary.

Date evidence: live documentation; the exact configuration described here was not established from a dated pre-cutoff version.

### 3. RFC 9700: restricted tokens and a hardened OAuth authorization flow

URL: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9700

Use this security baseline to limit token consequences: restrict access-token audiences and privileges, use authorization code flow with PKCE where applicable, and protect refresh tokens with client binding, rotation, or sender constraint. Its audience rule specifically requires a resource server to reject a token intended for a different resource server.

Caveat: PKCE protects the code exchange; it is not a cure for theft of an already-issued bearer token or an authenticated browser session. Every application must enforce the relevant checks. The document is a standard, not evidence that a particular deployment already implements it.

Date evidence: RFC 9700 was published in January 2025, before the cutoff.

### 4. Authentik User Login stage: bound the shared identity-provider session

URL: https://docs.goauthentik.io/add-secure-apps/flows-stages/stages/user_login/

This component exposes the lifetime and reuse controls for the Authentik session itself, including session duration, remember-me extension, termination of other sessions, and optional network or location binding. These are directly relevant to the credential whose compromise could enable fresh logins to several applications.

Caveat: the documentation explicitly separates termination of Authentik sessions from OAuth refresh tokens. Browser-session cookies may survive browser behavior that users interpret as closing the browser, and location binding is not cryptographic replay prevention. Set and test the identity-provider session, application session, and token lifetimes separately.

Date evidence: live documentation, with no dated version opened to establish these exact details before the cutoff.

### 5. WebAuthn Level 2: origin-scoped public-key authentication

URL: https://www.w3.org/TR/2021/REC-webauthn-2-20210408/

WebAuthn provides public-key credentials scoped to the relying party, making it a useful stronger authentication mechanism at the central identity provider or independently at especially sensitive applications. Its origin and credential scoping address credential phishing rather than relying only on a reusable password or manually entered one-time code. Authentik's current validation-stage documentation supports WebAuthn and a user-verification requirement.

Caveat: protecting the authentication ceremony does not invalidate an already-stolen authenticated session. Enrollment, spare authenticators, and recovery need to preserve the same security objective. Independent registration at an application requires that application's support.

Date evidence: the opened W3C Recommendation is dated 8 April 2021, before the cutoff; the separate Authentik integration evidence is live documentation.

### 6. OpenID Connect Back-Channel Logout 1.0: propagate session termination

URL: https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-backchannel-1_0.html

This protocol gives the identity provider a direct server-to-server mechanism for asking relying applications to terminate sessions, which can make central incident response more useful after session theft or account compromise. It addresses the gap between ending the identity-provider session and ending each application's own session.

Caveat: the relying application must implement session termination and expose a logout endpoint reachable by the provider. It does not automatically revoke every independent bearer token. Confirm support and behavior for each installed application and provider version.

Date evidence: the opened specification incorporates errata set 1 and is dated 15 December 2023, before the cutoff.

### 7. RFC 9449 DPoP: make a stolen token insufficient by itself

URL: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9449

DPoP is an alternative to ordinary bearer-token replay semantics: the client proves possession of a private key and the recipient verifies the token's binding to that key. It can reduce the value of a leaked access or refresh token when the attacker has not also obtained the corresponding key or control of the client.

Caveat: this requires compatible clients, authorization servers, and resource servers. I did not establish that the user's Authentik deployment or applications support it, and it does not protect an unrelated Authentik browser cookie.

Date evidence: RFC 9449 was published in September 2023, before the cutoff.

## How I would use this shortlist

For a practical comparison, trace four independent paths: a compromised service account, a stolen application's token/session, a stolen Authentik session, and compromise of Authentik's administrative authority. For each, identify which other applications become accessible, whether another factor is required, and how access is revoked. This is a design review framework rather than a claim about a tested installation.

The most immediately transferable controls are separate application registrations, mandatory MFA with suitable recovery, recipient-restricted tokens, explicit session lifetimes, and verified logout behavior. Keeping additional local authentication for a particularly sensitive application is a reasonable isolation option if that application's access path actually enforces it. Federation can improve consistency and management while concentrating trust; retaining independent credentials trades that concentration for more separate authentication and recovery systems to maintain.

All seven candidate sources were opened. An unauthenticated grep.app code-search attempt failed; a public GitHub source page was subsequently found through web search and opened, so that is code-through-web evidence, not native code-search success. Current Authentik documentation and main-branch code are not treated as proof of March 2025 behavior. No deployment, exploit test, or empirical security comparison was performed.
